os-diagnostics-data.title: Diagnostics store
os-diagnostics-data.summary: The database behind OS.Diagnostics: errors go into their own `DiagnosticsDb` on any OS.EFCore provider, secrets and personal data are masked before they are written, old rows are removed every day, and an `IErrorReader` gives you everything an error inbox page needs.

gives.1: Its own small database, so a broken main database never stops you from seeing why it broke. A separate SQLite file is enough, and it can be encrypted.
gives.2: Passwords, bearer tokens, emails, card numbers and national IDs are masked before a row is written, with check digits so ordinary numbers stay readable.
gives.3: A failing store never reports into itself, so a full disk or a dropped server cannot start an endless loop of errors about errors.

sample.quick: Errors in a SQLite file next to the app
sample.encrypted: An encrypted error file with two weeks of history

start.title: Getting started
start.summary: Register the store, give `DiagnosticsDb` a provider and create its table once.

2.title: One call
2.text: `AddOSDiagnosticsData` also registers the reader and a daily cleanup.

3.title: Separate context
3.text: Errors live in `DiagnosticsDb`, apart from the main database.

4.title: Tables not created
4.text: The table is not created for you.

1.title: Registering
1.text:
OS.Diagnostics collects errors through `IErrorSink` and hands them in batches to an `IErrorStore`. This package is that store.

`AddOSDiagnosticsData` registers it, together with the `IErrorReader` and a daily retention job, and each call replaces the previous one. If `AddOSDiagnostics` has not been called yet, it registers that too, so one call is enough.

Only `AppCode` still has to be set with `AddOSDiagnostics(o => o.AppCode = "shop")`, in either order.

2.title: Context and why separate
2.text:
The rows live in `DiagnosticsDb`, a context of the package's own. You register it with any OS.EFCore provider exactly as you would your own context, for example with `AddOSSqlite<DiagnosticsDb>(o => o.Path = "data/errors.db")` in your setup.

Keeping errors in a separate database is deliberate. When the main database is down, that is exactly when you need to read the errors, and a small SQLite file next to the app keeps working.

3.title: Creating the table
3.text: The table is not created for you. Call `EnsureCreatedAsync` once at startup. If you use migrations, add them with the option `--context DiagnosticsDb` in your command.

4.title: Writing batches
4.text:
Each batch is written with a plain `SaveChangesAsync` on purpose, and `SaveAsync` is not used. The reason is that `SaveAsync` reports busy and offline databases to `IErrorSink`. Doing that from the store itself would feed its own failures back into the queue.

A failed batch is logged by the writer and dropped. Every date is stored in UTC.

register.title: Register everything
register.note: `AddOSDiagnostics` collects, `AddOSDiagnosticsData` stores, in either order; the provider call registers OS.EFCore itself.

create-table.title: Create the table at startup
create-table.note: Run this once before the app starts serving; with migrations, use `MigrateAsync` instead.

round-trip.title: What one row holds
round-trip.note: The id, app code, fingerprint, type, request, user and the time, which comes back in UTC.

type.DiagnosticsDb: The package's own context. Register it with a provider; it holds one table of errors.
type.ErrorEntry: One stored error: one row per report that passed the rate limit.

DiagnosticsDataEx.AddOSDiagnosticsData: Registers the store, the reader and the retention job, and validates the options at once. A second call replaces the first.

DiagnosticsDb.DiagnosticsDb: Created by the provider registration; you do not create it yourself.
DiagnosticsDb.PurgeErrorsAsync: Removes rows older than the given time in batches of 1000 and returns how many were removed (`data.notFound` when there were none). The retention job uses it; you can call it from an admin page too.

ErrorEntry.Id: Database key, growing with every row.
ErrorEntry.AppCode: Which app wrote the row, from `DiagnosticsOptions.AppCode`.
ErrorEntry.TraceId: The request's trace id, the one the user sees on the error page. Indexed, so a trace is found at once.
ErrorEntry.ErrorType: Full name of the exception type.
ErrorEntry.Fingerprint: 16 characters that identify the problem: same type and same place in your code give the same fingerprint.
ErrorEntry.Source: Where the error came from, for example `efcore:save` or a hook's name.
ErrorEntry.Message: The exception message after masking, at most 500 characters. Stored exactly, without text normalization.
ErrorEntry.StackTrace: The stack after masking, cut by `DiagnosticsOptions.MaxStack`. Stored exactly.
ErrorEntry.Method: HTTP method of the request, if there was one.
ErrorEntry.Route: Route of the request after masking, at most 256 characters.
ErrorEntry.StatusCode: HTTP status that was returned, or 0.
ErrorEntry.UserId: Id of the signed-in user, if any; used to count affected users.
ErrorEntry.Suppressed: How many reports of the same problem the rate limit held back just before this one. Counts include them.
ErrorEntry.OccurredAt: When the error happened, always in UTC.

inbox.title: Reading the inbox
inbox.summary: Issues, one issue in detail, a trace, a summary and the error types, all as `OSResult` values.

1.title: Rows to issues
1.text: Rows with the same fingerprint count as one issue.

2.title: Issue list
2.text: `IssuesAsync` returns the issues of the last hours, newest first.

3.title: Find by trace
3.text: `FindAsync` turns a support ticket's trace id into its issue.

4.title: No exceptions
4.text: When the database cannot be read, the answer is `Unavailable`.

1.title: The issue list
1.text:
The reader turns rows into issues: rows with the same fingerprint are one issue.

`IssuesAsync` looks at the last `Hours`, 24 by default and never longer than the retention. It reads at most `ScanLimit` of the newest rows in that window and returns at most `MaxIssues` issues.

Issues come newest first. Each has its count (suppressed reports included), affected users, first and last time and 24 bars for a small chart.

2.title: New and details
2.text:
`FirstDate` is the first time ever, not only in the window. So an issue is `IsNew` only when it really started within `NewHours`.

`GetIssueAsync` gives one issue with its latest message and the `SampleLimit` newest occurrences. Pass a trace to jump to that occurrence, which is then put first and returned as `Found`.

The stack is only read when you pass `withStack: true`, so you can show it to admins only.

3.title: Search and summary
3.text:
`FindAsync` turns a trace id from a support ticket into its issue. Spaces and line breaks around a pasted trace are ignored.

`SummaryAsync` and `TypesAsync` feed a dashboard tile and a type filter.

4.title: When the database fails
4.text: When the database cannot be read, every method returns `Unavailable` with the code `diagnostics.unavailable` instead of throwing. The reader never reports to `IErrorSink`.

issues.title: The issue list
issues.note: The occurrence from three days ago is outside the window, so the count is 2, but it still makes the issue not new.

detail.title: One issue, jumping to a trace
detail.note: The stack is hidden and the wanted trace is in the samples.

find-and-summary.title: Find a trace, then summarize
find-and-summary.note: The pasted trace had spaces around it; they do not matter.

admin-page.title: Show the stack to admins only
admin-page.note: A stack trace can reveal paths and internals, so `withStack` follows the user's role.

privacy.title: Secrets and personal data
privacy.summary: What is masked before a row is written, what is left alone on purpose, and how to add your own patterns.

1.title: Automatic masking
1.text: Secrets and personal data are replaced with `***` before a row is written.

2.title: Built-in patterns
2.text: Passwords, tokens, emails, card numbers and national IDs are masked.

4.title: A safety net
4.text: Masking is a safety net, not permission.

1.title: What is masked
1.text:
Exception messages often carry what should never reach a log table: a connection string, a token, a customer's email. Before a row is written, the message, the stack and the route are scanned and these are replaced with `***`.

The value after `Password=`, `Pwd=` or `"password":` is masked. So is a `Bearer` token and anything shaped like a JWT. Email addresses are masked too.

16-digit card numbers (spaces or dashes allowed) are masked when they pass the Luhn check. 10-digit numbers are masked when they pass the Iranian national ID check. Persian digits count too.

2.title: Why checks
2.text:
The checks are there to keep ordinary numbers readable: an order number or a 16-digit id that fails the check stays as it is.

They are not perfect, and the honest trade is to mask too much rather than too little. About one random 10-digit number in eleven passes the national ID check, so a Unix time such as 1760000000 can be masked. So can a word after `password:` in a sentence.

3.title: Your own patterns
3.text:
Add your own patterns with `ScrubPatterns`. Each one must have a match timeout, because a pattern that runs away would block the writer.

If any pattern runs out of time, the whole field is stored as `***`, never unmasked.

4.title: Safety net
4.text:
Masking happens before the 500-character cut, so a row never ends up longer than its column.

Masking is a safety net, not permission. Keep secrets out of exception messages in the first place.

scrubbed.title: What reaches the table
scrubbed.note: The email, the password, the card and the national ID are masked; the rest of the sentence is kept.

left-alone.title: Ordinary numbers stay, with one known exception
left-alone.note: The order number fails the check and stays; the Unix time happens to pass it and is masked.

custom-pattern.title: Add your own pattern
custom-pattern.note: Always give the `Regex` a timeout; without one the options are rejected.

retention.title: Retention
retention.summary: Old rows are removed every day; keep them longer, forever, or purge by hand.

1.title: Daily cleanup
1.text: Rows older than `RetentionDays` days are removed.

2.title: Small batches
2.text: Deleting happens in batches of 1000 so no long lock is held.

1.title: The cleanup job
1.text:
A background job removes rows older than `RetentionDays`, 30 by default. It runs one minute after the app starts and then every `PurgeEvery`, which is one day.

It deletes in batches of 1000 through `PurgeErrorsAsync`, so a large table never holds one long lock. Set `RetentionDays` to 0 to keep everything; the job then does nothing.

2.title: Failures and the reader
2.text:
A failed purge is logged and tried again at the next run. Because the purge uses the normal OS.EFCore path, a database that is down is also reported once to `IErrorSink`. That is safe, because the store, not the purge, is what the writer calls.

The reader never looks further back than the retention, so a 30-day store answers at most 720 hours.

purge.title: Purge by hand
purge.note: Two rows were older than 30 days; one is left.

keep-longer.title: Keep three months, purge every six hours
keep-longer.note: A shorter `PurgeEvery` keeps each run small on a busy app.

keep-forever.title: Keep everything
keep-forever.note: Only for small apps: the table then grows forever.

options.title: Options
options.summary: Retention, reader limits, the table name and your own masking patterns.

1.title: Checked at start
1.text: A wrong value stops the app at startup, not at the first error.

2.title: Reader limits
2.text: Reader limits keep the admin page fast.

3.title: Error table
3.text: `Table` lets errors share a database with other tables.

1.title: Checking options
1.text: All options are checked when you call `AddOSDiagnosticsData`, so a wrong value stops the app at startup, not at the first error.

2.title: Reader limits
2.text:
The reader limits keep an admin page fast however many errors there are.

`ScanLimit` caps how many rows one issue list reads. `MaxIssues` caps how many issues it returns. `SampleLimit` caps how many occurrences one issue shows.

3.title: Table name
3.text:
`Table` lets the errors share a database with other tables. It must be a plain name: only letters, digits and the character `_` are allowed, and it starts with a letter.

It is read once, when the model is first built.

defaults.title: The defaults
defaults.note: Good for most apps; raise the limits only when the page needs it.

bad-table.title: A table name that is not a plain name
bad-table.note: Rejected at registration, before anything touches the database.

busy-app.title: A busier app
busy-app.note: More rows per scan and more samples, in a table of its own name.

type.DiagnosticsDataOptions: Retention, reader limits, the table name and extra masking patterns.

DiagnosticsDataOptions.RetentionDays: How many days rows are kept. 30 by default; 0 keeps everything.
DiagnosticsDataOptions.PurgeEvery: How often old rows are removed. One day by default; at least one minute.
DiagnosticsDataOptions.ScanLimit: At most this many of the newest rows are read for one issue list. 5000 by default.
DiagnosticsDataOptions.MaxIssues: At most this many issues in a list, and at most this many error types. 100 by default.
DiagnosticsDataOptions.SampleLimit: How many recent occurrences one issue shows. 20 by default.
DiagnosticsDataOptions.NewHours: An issue whose first occurrence is newer than this many hours is new. 24 by default.
DiagnosticsDataOptions.Table: Table name, `Errors` by default. Letters, digits and `_` only, starting with a letter.
DiagnosticsDataOptions.ScrubPatterns: Your own patterns to mask, added after the built-in ones. Each needs a match timeout.
